item.command:
/bin/bash -lc "cat > '/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec8/luna/followup.tsv' <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.42.5	hearing gives way to sight	The commentary begins from detecting by sight or hearing and ends with confirmation; Job says he had heard of God by the ear but now his eye sees. This is an explicit passage from received report to firsthand perception.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Kgs.10.6	report confirmed as true	The commentary glosses haqq as correspondence and confirmation; the Queen of Sheba tells Solomon that the report she heard in her land was true. Her own assessment names a report matched by what she encounters.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Kgs.10.7	belief after seeing	The commentary permits a sight-before-confirmation reading but says the Qur'anic wording does not prove it; the Queen says she did not believe the reports until she came and saw with her own eyes. This is an explicit biblical instance of that sequence.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Kgs.3.26	the response tests the claim	The commentary links verification with becoming certain about an affair; Solomon's proposed division of the child elicits different responses from the two women. Their reactions supply evidence for identifying the true mother.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Kgs.3.27	judgment after examination	The commentary's gloss of haqq includes verifying a matter; Solomon rules that the child belongs to the woman who pleaded for its life. The verse gives the conclusion of a specific test of competing claims.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.1.30	acts seen before the refusal	The commentary allows sight to lead to belief but says that reading is not established by the surah's flat wording; Moses recalls that Israel saw the LORD fight for them in Egypt. This supplies concrete witnessed evidence before the next verse records disbelief.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.1.32	disbelief despite witnessed acts	The commentary's sequence can be read as seeing then confirming, but does not require it; Moses says Israel still did not trust the LORD after recalling those works before their eyes. It is a direct counterexample to sight automatically producing belief.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.6.9	seeing without perceiving	The commentary says loss need not mean blindness and the exception need not mean sight; Isaiah is explicitly told that people will hear without understanding and see without perceiving. This gives the proposed sensory reading an explicit prophetic parallel.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.6.10	eyes and ears shut	The commentary leaves blindness as an unproven reading; Isaiah describes dull hearts, heavy ears, and shut eyes, with turning and healing as the alternative. The passage makes sensory incapacity a judgment rather than a fact implied by loss alone.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.5.21	eyes that do not see	The commentary warns against inferring blindness from the simple statement of loss; Jeremiah addresses a foolish people with eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear. It is another explicit prophetic formulation of that image.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.12.2	seeing and hearing without response	The commentary says the surah does not itself state that humanity is blind; Ezekiel calls Israel a rebellious house with eyes to see but not seeing and ears to hear but not hearing. The text names the interpretive condition directly.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.3.4	a voice from the fire	The commentary cites Musa's sight of fire and notes that the root's range includes hearing; in Exodus, the LORD calls Moses from the bush and Moses answers. This continues the same encounter through an auditory summons.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.4.31	hearing, believing, and worshipping	The commentary links perception, confirmation, and action; Israel hears that the LORD has visited them, believes, and bows in worship. This gives the sensory-to-assent sequence a communal outcome.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.27.13	belief before seeing	The commentary allows a sight-to-belief reading but does not make it necessary; the psalmist says he believes he will see the LORD's goodness. This reverses the proposed order and ties faith to hoped-for sight.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.7.9	belief and firmness in one saying	The commentary defines iman as confirmation and haqq as becoming sure; Isaiah says that without believing, the hearers will not be established. The verse makes trust and firmness a deliberate Hebrew wordplay.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:2Chr.20.20	trust in God and prophets	The commentary glosses iman as accepting a report as true; Jehoshaphat tells Judah to believe in God and his prophets, linking belief with being established and prospering. It applies assent to both divine and prophetic speech.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.89.2	faithfulness proclaimed by mouth	The commentary reads mutual counsel as passing confirmed truth among people; the psalmist says his mouth will make God's faithfulness known to every generation. This is oral transmission across time rather than a private conviction.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.17.12	hands held steady together	The commentary ends with people urging one another to patience; Aaron and Hur hold up Moses' hands until sunset so he can persist. The scene gives collective support a concrete role in endurance.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.1.32	not trusting after God's care	The commentary's iman means assent; Moses says Israel did not trust God after recalling how God carried them. The verse adds a relational failure to the sight-and-disbelief contrast.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Sanhedrin 5:1	seven interrogations of witnesses	The commentary's Yusuf and news examples turn on whether a report is credible; the Mishnah specifies interrogations for witnesses in capital cases. It makes verification a formal procedure rather than an intuition.
strong	tevrat	motif	Susanna (Theodotion) 51-59	separating and testing witnesses	The commentary cites checking a report before accepting it; Daniel separates the two elders and asks each where they saw Susanna, exposing their incompatible answers. This is a narrative of cross-examination overturning false testimony.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 27:5	speech as a test	The commentary glosses confirming a matter and also develops hearing; Sirach compares testing a person in conversation to testing pottery in a furnace. Speech becomes evidence of character.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 27:7	hear before praising	The commentary connects hearing with verifying what is true; Sirach warns against praising someone before hearing them speak, since this is how people are tested. It gives listening an explicit evidentiary role.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 27:6	words reveal inner cultivation	The commentary says the mind works and the confirmed truth is conveyed; Sirach compares fruit revealing a tree's cultivation with words revealing the thought of a person's heart. It links outward speech to inward disposition.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.7.16	fruit tests a prophet	The commentary pairs belief with righteous deeds and treats truth as something confirmed; Jesus says false prophets are recognized by their fruits. Conduct becomes a test of a religious claim.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.2.13	doers rather than hearers	The commentary begins with seeing or hearing and then names righteous action; Paul says hearers of the law are not righteous, but doers will be justified. It makes response in action decisive.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.10.17	faith comes through hearing	The commentary notes that perception includes hearing and glosses iman as assent; Paul says faith comes from hearing the message. This gives the hearing-to-belief sequence a direct Christian formulation.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.4.39	belief from another's report	The commentary's Yusuf scene concerns whether to credit another person's words; many Samaritans first believe because of the woman's testimony about Jesus. This is a specific instance of received speech producing belief.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.4.42	hearing for oneself	The commentary links heard claims with confirmation; the Samaritans say they now believe not merely because of the woman's speech, since they have heard Jesus themselves and know. The narrative moves from report to firsthand confirmation.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.24.11	a report first disbelieved	The commentary cites a report that a listener might reject; the apostles treat the women's account of the empty tomb as nonsense and do not believe them. This is a Gospel scene of a true report meeting disbelief.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.24.12	inspection after the report	The commentary connects verification with seeing what is there; Peter runs to the tomb, sees the linen cloths, and marvels after the women's report. The verse adds physical inspection to the disputed testimony.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.20.27	invitation to inspect	The commentary allows sight to function as verification; Jesus invites Thomas to see and touch his wounds and tells him to become believing. This is a direct scene of testing testimony through sensory evidence.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.20.28	confession after encounter	The commentary says iman joins assent to what is found true; Thomas answers Jesus with a confession after the invitation to inspect. This gives the sensory encounter its explicit verbal affirmation.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.20.31	written testimony intended to produce belief	The commentary's chain includes truth communicated to others; John says the signs are written so readers may believe and have life. The verse makes a written report the means of later assent.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.1.22	doers, not hearers alone	The commentary moves from hearing or seeing to righteous action; James commands readers to be doers of the word, not hearers only who deceive themselves. It makes perception without action a self-deception.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Exod.4.31	ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary labels iman from ء م ن; Exodus uses the Hebrew אמנ root when Israel believes after hearing that God has visited them. The proposed correspondence links the root to the heard report.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Deut.1.32	ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary glosses iman as tasdiq; Moses says Israel did not believe the LORD, using the Hebrew אמנ root. The root occurs in a scene where remembered evidence still fails to produce trust.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Isa.7.9	ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary's iman is confirmation; Isaiah repeats forms of the Hebrew אמנ root for believing and being established. The table's sound correspondence is unverified, while the Hebrew wordplay itself is explicit.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:2Chr.20.20	ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary labels iman with ء م ن; Jehoshaphat uses the Hebrew אמנ root for believing God and the prophets. The proposed cognate appears in a direct exhortation about trust.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Exod.17.12	ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary pairs iman with patience; Exodus uses אמונה for Moses' hands remaining steady while Aaron and Hur support him. This root use emphasizes firmness and endurance rather than assent.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.89.2	ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary's haqq is truth passed among people; the psalm uses אמונה for God's faithfulness that the speaker announces by mouth to later generations. The possible cognate adds the sense of reliable fidelity.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.27.13	ء م ن / אמנ; table sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary glosses iman as confirmation; the psalm uses the Hebrew אמנ root for believing before seeing the promised goodness. The candidate shows a different temporal relation between faith and sight.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.8.5	ء ن س / אנש; BDB-cited Arabic cognate in table	The commentary labels al-insan with ء ن س; the psalm uses אנוש for mortal humanity, yet says God remembers and crowns it with glory. The proposed cognate adds a counter-image of human dignity beside loss.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Dan.7.13	ء ن س / Aramaic אנש; table sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary's word label is al-insan; Daniel's Aramaic vision has a figure like a son of man receiving dominion. The proposed cognate shows the root in an exalted, not merely frail, human-like figure.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.90.11	ع م ل / עמל; table sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary labels righteous deeds with ع م ل; the psalm uses עמל for the toil and sorrow of human years, which quickly pass. The possible root link adds mortal labor under the surah's language of loss.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.27.13	belief looking toward future sight	The commentary's suggested movement is from seeing to confirmation but is not required; the psalmist believes in order to see the LORD's goodness. The verse preserves the reverse order as a distinct reading.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.17.12	sustaining another's endurance	The commentary's final injunction is reciprocal counsel in patience; Aaron and Hur each support Moses so his hands stay raised through the battle. It depicts endurance sustained through another's help.
medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Matt.13.13	parables and failed perception	The commentary says blindness is not established by its plain wording; Jesus explains that he speaks in parables because people see without seeing and hear without hearing. This Christian interpretation makes the sensory failure explicit.
medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Matt.13.14	Isaiah applied to hearers	The commentary leaves the blindness reading as an interpretive possibility; Matthew says Isaiah's prophecy is fulfilled in hearers who do not understand. It records a Christian application of the prophetic sensory formula.
medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Matt.13.15	closed eyes and possible healing	The commentary contrasts loss with a possible process of seeing and testing; Matthew's quotation says closed eyes prevent seeing, understanding, turning, and being healed. It gives that reading a concrete Christian interpretive context.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.13.16	blessed eyes that see	The commentary allows the exception to be read as seeing, while noting the surah does not prove it; Jesus calls the disciples' seeing eyes and hearing ears blessed. This is an explicit positive counterpart to failed perception.
medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:John.12.40	Isaiah explains unbelief after signs	The commentary says seeing does not necessarily establish belief; John says that despite Jesus' signs, some did not believe, and cites Isaiah's blinded eyes and hardened heart. It supplies a Christian interpretation of failed response to visible evidence.
medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Acts.28.26	Isaiah's hearing formula applied by Paul	The commentary leaves sensory failure as an unproven reading; Paul quotes Isaiah's command to hear without understanding and see without perceiving when addressing his Roman hearers. This is a later Christian application of the same formula.
medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Acts.28.27	dull heart and refusal to turn	The commentary's possible reading links perception with return and testing; Paul continues Isaiah's words about a dull heart, closed ears, and eyes, lest hearers turn and be healed. It makes the consequence of failed perception explicit.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.1.8	belief without seeing	The commentary says its text does not establish that belief follows sight; Peter says his readers love and believe in Christ though they have not seen him. This is another direct Christian formulation of faith without sight.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.1.23	a face seen in a mirror	The commentary cites the eye's small visible likeness in its pupil; James compares a hearer who does not act to someone looking at their face in a mirror. The image links seeing oneself with hearing a word.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.1.24	seeing and then forgetting	The commentary develops a tiny image seen and then a process of confirmation; James says the mirror-gazer leaves and forgets what he saw. The verse gives a specific failure to retain what perception disclosed.
medium	tevrat	motif	Sirach 27:6	fruit reveals cultivation	The commentary joins inward mental work with outward truth; Sirach says fruit reveals a tree's cultivation just as speech reveals the thought of the heart. This makes observable expression evidence of inner character.
weak	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Job.42.6	Job's response after seeing; wording debated	The commentary joins verification with the soul's submission to truth; after Job says he now sees God, he withdraws or repents. The final Hebrew clause is difficult, so the link between sight and changed posture is tentative.
EOF"

medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Acts.28.26	Isaiah's hearing formula applied by Paul	The commentary leaves sensory failure as an unproven reading; Paul quotes Isaiah's command to hear without understanding and see without perceiving when addressing his Roman hearers. medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Acts.28.27	dull heart and refusal to turn	The commentary's possible reading links perception with return and testing; Paul continues Isaiah's words about a dull heart, closed ears, and eyes, lest hearers turn and be healed. medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.1.8	belief without seeing	The commentary says its text does not establish that belief follows sight; Peter says his readers love and believe in Christ though they have not seen him. This is another direct Christian formulation of faith without sight.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.1.23	a face seen in a mirror	The commentary cites the eye's small visible likeness in its pupil; James compares a hearer who does not act to someone looking at their face in a mirror. The image links seeing oneself with hearing a word.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.1.24	seeing and then forgetting	The commentary develops a tiny image seen and then a process of confirmation; James says the mirror-gazer leaves and forgets what he saw. The verse gives a specific failure to retain what perception disclosed.
medium	tevrat	motif	Sirach 27:6	fruit reveals cultivation	The commentary joins inward mental work with outward truth; Sirach says fruit reveals a tree's cultivation just as speech reveals the thought of the heart. This makes observable expression evidence of inner character.
